subject: Biology
title: Biofilms: Bacterial Cities
description: A short lesson to help you apply Biofilms: Bacterial Cities.

hook.text: Bacteria don't always float alone. Many build slimy communities called biofilms.

buildup.text: Dental plaque is a biofilm—layers of bacteria cemented to your teeth in a sticky matrix.

discovery.text: Inside a biofilm, bacteria communicate using chemical signals in a process called quorum sensing.

twist.text: Biofilms are up to 1,000 times more resistant to antibiotics than free-floating bacteria.

climax.text: They coat medical implants, water pipes, and ship hulls—a persistent challenge for engineers.

punchline.text: Even bacteria prefer to live in communities.

quiz.question: What makes biofilms dangerous in medical settings?
options: They are far more resistant to antibiotics

details.summary: Biofilms are structured communities of bacteria encased in a self-produced sticky matrix of sugars and proteins. Living in biofilms gives bacteria up to 1,000 times greater antibiotic resistance than free-floating cells, making infections involving biofilms extremely difficult to treat.
details.whyItMatters: Biofilms cause most chronic bacterial infections and contaminate medical devices from catheters to artificial joints. Understanding biofilm biology is essential for developing strategies against persistent, hard-to-treat infections.
takeaways: Biofilms make bacteria up to 1,000 times more resistant to antibiotics
Over 80 percent of chronic bacterial infections involve biofilm formation
Dental plaque is one of the most familiar everyday examples of a biofilm

faq.question: Why are biofilms so resistant to antibiotics?
faq.answer: The sticky matrix blocks antibiotic penetration. Bacteria deep inside receive fewer nutrients and grow slowly, making them less susceptible. Biofilms also contain persister cells that enter dormant states completely immune to antibiotics that target actively growing cells.

faq.question: Where do biofilms form in the human body?
faq.answer: On teeth as dental plaque, in chronic wounds, on medical implants and catheters, in the lungs of cystic fibrosis patients, and in urinary tract infections. Biofilms on medical devices are a leading cause of hospital-acquired infections worldwide.
